2 | MATERIALS AND METHODS
In S06_Extended Methods, we present an unabridged version of this
Methods section.
2.1 | Mock soup preparation
2.1.1 | Input species
We used Malaise traps to collect arthropods in Gaoligong Mountain,
Yunnan province, China. From these, we selected 282 individuals
that represented different morphospecies, and from each individual,
we separately extracted DNA from the leg and the body. After clus-
tering, we ended up with two hundred and forty-­
eight 97%-­
similarity
DNA barcodes, which we used as the ‘input species’ for the mock
soups (S07_MTBFAS.fasta).
decisions.reason: Berry2011positively reports empirical tag-dependent amplification/reproducibility effects, so it is not excluded as mere methods theory. Complete O'Donnell2016primary explicitly reviews Berry's one-step indexed-primer bias and two-step remedy, empirically re-tests the effect with replicate environmental samples/index tags, and reports the community reproducibility contrast. Current explicitly co-cites both for the same tested tag-bias hypothesis and tests same-versus-different tag reproducibility, without separately testing a Berry-specific T-RFLP finding or an additional intervention. Under the closest empirical-chain rule select O'Donnell2016once for this current comparison rather than also exporting the2011ancestor. This is not alternate-report/data equivalence, and distinct original samples or marker/method changes alone neither establish an extra pair nor exclude conceptual retesting. The raw independent2011positive opinion remains unchanged. Existing2328Elbrecht2017targets a different pipeline/error-reduction comparison and does not represent the tag-bias target.

decisions.reason: O'Donnell et al. (2016; 10.1371/journal.pone.0148698) empirically tested 1-step PCR with twin 5' sample-identifying nucleotide index tags and post-PCR adapter ligation across annealing temperatures (46 C and 51 C), finding that different primer index tags induce template-specific amplification bias across technical replicates of the same DNA extract. Yang et al. (2021) likewise use twin 5' sample-identifying primer tags with post-PCR adapter ligation and conduct an explicit 1-step PCR 'Tag-bias test' (Section 1, p. 1149; Methods 2.1.9, p. 1152; Results 3.4, Fig. 3, and Figs. S3-S4, pp. 1153-1154) comparing community NMDS ordinations between pairs using the same tags versus different tags under optimal, high-annealing-temperature, and touchdown PCR protocols, explicitly citing O'Donnell et al. (2016) for this hypothesis. Although Yang et al. do not test O'Donnell et al.'s two-step PCR remedy, they conceptually re-test its core 1-step tag-bias finding, which is absent from shipped_rows.

4.1 | Co-­
designed wet-­
lab and bioinformatic
methods to remove errors
The Begum workflow co-­
designs the wet-­
lab and bioinformatic com-
ponents (Figure 1) (Zepeda-­
Mendoza et al., 2016) to minimize multi-
ple sources of error (Table 1). Apart from the use of qPCR to optimize
PCR conditions, the wet-­
lab and bioinformatic components are de-
signed to work together. Twin-­
tagging allows removal of tag jumps,
which result in sample misassignments. Multiple, independent PCRs
per sample allow removal of false-­
positive sequences caused by
PCR and sequencing error and by low-­
level contamination, at the

decisions.reason: Inspecting McLaren et al. (2019; 10.7554/eLife.46923) alongside Yang et al. (2021) shows that McLaren et al. propose and test a stagewise multiplicative-bias model in which protocol- and taxon-specific bias is invariant in taxon ratios across sample compositions and can be calibrated using control communities. Yang et al. do not test multiplicative ratio invariance, stagewise bias partitioning, or calibration; instead, they fit uncalibrated linear regressions of input genomic DNA concentration on raw OTU read counts across evenness and tissue treatments (Methods 2.1.9; Results 3.2) and cite McLaren et al. (2019) as background mechanism (Section 1, p. 1149) and as 'the conventional wisdom that OTU size is a poor predictor of species relative abundances' (Discussion Section 4, p. 1157), in contrast to their explicit targeted replication of Elbrecht et al. (2017), which is already represented by shipped row 2328.
